name: Kira Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a four-person agency on the market square, upstairs from a solicitor. We brand small rural businesses: farm shops, a cider maker, a riding school, the butcher who wants to look 'heritage'. I use AI every day for first drafts, moodboards and writing the little brand stories on the back of the packaging, then I spend the afternoon making it look less like AI.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy sitting in a farm kitchen hearing why their granddad started the place, then turning that into a logo. Tough part is I'm still junior, Helen, my boss, rewrites half my client emails. And I'm on low pay with about a week and a half saved. My partner Owen is a mechanic at the tractor dealer, so we're careful, but we're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold, and that's normal for any new thing. I'd say small businesses should still use it to save money. I'd post something like that on the agency's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me okay. I'm already the quickest with the tools, so I keep that edge, and the clients still want a person in the farm kitchen. My worry is just money, a week and a half in the bank isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and ask Helen if I can take a couple of clients myself, start to finish. I'd put fifty a week into savings. I'd start a small side job doing logos for church events and craft stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit impatient to get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're fine, but a week and a half isn't much. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. My partner Owen's wage from the tractor dealer is what keeps us steady, and my design pay is the extra, so we're fine until something breaks. If the tractor dealer cut Owen's hours, we'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the agency would you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lewis, who does our print artwork and file checks. Even the small tools take some of that. He's not keen on change, and he's got a little one at home.

I'd tell small businesses to **still use it** to save money.
think: I keep my **edge** as the quickest with tools.
Clients still want a person in the **farm kitchen**.
My real worry is a **week and a half** of savings.
do: Ask Helen to let me run **two clients** start to finish.
Start **side work** doing logos for church events and craft stalls.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit **impatient** to get on.

fieldNote: She's comfortable with **AI tools** and loses little in a plateau.

She's **ambitious**: wants her own clients and a side business.

steps.text: Ask Helen (her boss) to give her two clients start to finish
Save fifty a week toward a two-month cushion
Design logos for church events and craft stalls on the side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work. Small businesses get cheaper branding, and designers who move fast get more clients. I'd not want the government protecting jobs that don't make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency shrinks, but that's my chance. A farm shop won't pay agency prices if one designer with AI can do it in a week. I could be the one designer with AI who does a farm shop's whole brand for half what our agency charges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own studio on the side within six months, charging half the agency price. I'd build a set of AI templates for farm shops and cafés. If it took off, I'd leave the agency within a year, with Helen's blessing if I can get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about leaving a wage, but excited. This is what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving a wage with a week and a half saved is a big risk. How would you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the agency job until the side work paid the rent for three months straight. Owen's wage covers food. And my mum would have us for Sunday dinner, she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about this world bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lewis, at the agency. He won't learn the tools and he's got a family. I'd want to offer him some print work if my studio grows.

fieldNote: She sees disruption as **opportunity**, consistent with her **free-market** views.

She thinks about a **colleague with a family**.

steps.text: Launch a side studio offering branding at half agency prices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone, me included. I'd say families and churches will matter more than ever. I'd still not want handouts as the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my studio idea dies. If AI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, the farm shops make their own brand. Owen's mechanic job lasts until about 2031, so we'd live on his wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on the studio idea and save every penny for two years. I'd ask the tractor dealer about parts and admin, though that goes too. I'd look at something hands-on, maybe sign-making with my uncle, until the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My whole plan just vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no handouts. Would that hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've always said no to handouts, but if half the town is out of work, I'd take help and not feel guilty about it. If everyone's out of work, it's not a handout, it's survival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's the earner now, and I'd hate it. He'd say good, because he's always wanted to be. Then I'd go and find something to do with my hands.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for anyone, me included.
I'd say **families and churches** matter more than handouts.
think: My **studio idea dies** if AI does all thinking work.
**Owen's wage** carries us until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Stop **spending on the studio** and save every penny.
Live on **Owen's wage** for two or three years.
S2.quote: I've always said no to handouts, but if half the town is out of work, I'd take help and not feel guilty about it.
fieldNote: Her **plan collapses** when AI replaces even fast designers.
Her **free-market views bend** when everyone is affected.
Her partner's **hands-on job** becomes the household's bridge.

steps.text: Stop spending on the studio idea and save everything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so work hard and be smart. I'd tell young designers to build their own clients. I'd also say look after your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is enough for my studio to make good money for three years, then wind down. I'd ride the tools while they help me. By 2031 I'd want a hands-on skill and some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the side studio within six months and push it hard. I'd save half of whatever it makes. In year three I'd start learning sign-making with my uncle on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I like having a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save half? That's a lot.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A studio built on AI only has a few good years before AI makes my studio pointless. I'd rather put money away while the going is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Owen change family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait on kids until 2030, then go for it with savings behind us. Owen's job lasts till 2034, so we'd have a cushion.

fieldNote: She plans to **profit early**, then exit before AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning for anyone willing to plan. I'd tell people to take responsibility and build something. I'd not expect the government to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a decade of building my business, then switching. I'd be 37 in 2036. I could have savings, a house, and a second skill by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the studio within a year and grow it slowly. I'd buy a small house with Owen in four or five years. I'd learn a hands-on trade before 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious about the end, but mostly up for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with ten years, every year AI gets better, the price of a logo drops, and my studio's income drops with it. And I don't know what anyone does after 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Lewis, part-time, for print work. That's the kind of thing I'd like to do, give someone a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my plan dies before it starts. What would help is low-cost loans for small businesses to switch, and apprenticeships for adults. Not handouts, but a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the farm shops. Farmers trust someone who sat in their kitchen and heard about their granddad, and I'd like to think a computer can't do that.

headlineQuote: Farmers trust someone who sat in their kitchen and heard about their granddad, and I'd like to think a computer can't do that.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old junior** designer branding farm shops at a market-square agency.
She uses **AI every day** and dreams of her own cheap, fast studio.
Her partner Owen is a **tractor mechanic**, whose wage keeps them steady.
She's **free-market** and family-focused, but would accept help if everyone were hit.
She's **uneasy** with slow change, and **alarmed** by fast AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her studio plan dies before it starts.
whatWouldHelp: **Low-cost loans** for small businesses and paid **adult apprenticeships**.
